Forms and Functions of Plants and animals
ROOT SYSTEM
The root system is the descending (growing downwards) portion of the plant axis. When a seed germinates, radicle is the first organ to come out of it. It elongates to form primary or the tap root. It gives off lateral branches (secondary and tertiary roots) and thus forms the root system. Its branches penetrate through large and deep areas in the soil and anchor the plant very firmly. It also plays another vital role of absorbing water and mineral salts from the soil and transporting them upwards. How is the root suited in structure to carry out such functions? You shall learn in this lesson.
summary: The root system of a plant is the underground part of the plant that grows downward. It begins with the radicle emerging from the seed during germination, forming the primary or tap root, which then develops lateral branches to create a complex network of roots. This extensive root system not only secures the plant but also efficiently absorbs water and mineral salts from the soil, transporting them upward to the rest of the plant.

text: Root systems are mainly of two types:
summary: Root systems in plants are primarily classified into two types: taproot systems and fibrous root systems. Taproot systems feature a main primary root that grows downward, often accompanied by smaller lateral roots, while fibrous root systems consist of a dense mat of fine roots near the soil surface, lacking a dominant primary root.

summary: Dicot roots have an endodermis with closely packed, barrel-shaped cells that contain casparian strips and passage cells, facilitating the movement of water and salts into the xylem. The stele is located centrally and contains xylem patches arranged in a diarch to hexarch pattern. In contrast, monocot roots also have an endodermis with casparian strips and passage cells but lack the xylem patch arrangement seen in dicots; instead, the stele is simpler and more uniform.

text:
The roots grow in length with the help of apical meristem. It is called primary growth. Apart from primary growth, roots grow in width i.e., they increase in girth. This increase is called secondary growth. It is found only in dicot roots.
The tissues involved in secondary growth are lateral meristems i.e., vascular cambium and cork cambium.
It is important to remember that the vascular cambium and cork cambium are secondary in origin and arise from the pericycle.
Secondary growth is as follows-
Forms and Functions of Plants and animals
• Secondary tissue formed outer to the protoxylem bundle differentiates into prominent primary medullary ray thus, protoxylem does not get crushed (Fig. 6.11a).
Forms and Functions of Plants and animals
• Later, cork cambium (Phellogen) also differentiates in the pericycle (Fig. 6.11b).
summary: Roots grow in length through the apical meristem, a process known as primary growth. They also expand in diameter via secondary growth, driven by the vascular cambium and cork cambium, which form from the pericycle. This secondary growth prevents the protoxylem from being crushed by the expanding outer layers, and later, the cork cambium develops, contributing to the root's structure and function.
